transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic? What's been concerning you?

Oh, hello, Doctor. Thank you so much for taking the time to see me. I really hope I'm not taking up too much of your day. 

Well... I suppose what brings me in is just that, for the past year or so, I feel like I'm always... puttering. You know, fixing little things, arranging the house, or volunteering for just one more thing. I like to be helpful—and that's a good thing, isn't it? 

But... well, even at 87, I just have such a hard time sitting down and being still. I hope I'm explaining that right? I feel a little silly even bringing it up, honestly, because staying active is supposed to be a positive thing at my age, but it's just... I really can't seem to just sit and rest. Is that something I should be worried about?
When you're doing all this puttering and moving around, do you notice your heart racing, sweating, or a feeling of worry or nervousness—or is it more just a physical need to keep moving?

Oh, goodness, no. No, I don't get a racing heart or... or sweating, nothing like that. I don't feel worried at all, honestly. I'm actually quite cheerful when I'm up and about! 

It really is just... well, exactly what you said. Just a physical need to keep moving. Like my body just wants to go, even when I tell myself it's time to relax. I hope that makes sense? I really don't want you to think I'm having panic attacks or anything dreadful like that. I feel perfectly fine in my head, I just... I just can't seem to stay in my chair for very long. 

Is that a helpful answer? I want to make sure I'm giving you the right information.
Are you currently taking any medications? If so, could you tell me what they are?

Oh, medications? No, I'm actually not taking anything at all right now. I try very hard to take good care of myself—eating my vegetables and, well, keeping active, as I mentioned! So I don't have any prescriptions or... or daily pills to report. 

I know at my age, doctors usually expect a whole long list of things, so I hope it's not an inconvenience that I don't have one for you? I've just been very lucky with my health, really. Does that make things a bit easier for you, having a blank slate, so to speak?
Have you had any recent medical illnesses, infections, or health problems—even minor ones—in the past year or so, around the time this restlessness started?

Oh, no, no illnesses at all. I've been perfectly healthy, thank goodness! No infections, no trips to the hospital... not even a bad cold, really. 

Like I said, I've been very blessed with my health. I try to make sure I'm not a bother to the medical system, you know? I just try to eat right and keep my house tidy. So there hasn't been any sort of sickness or anything like that around the time this... puttering started. 

I hope that's alright? I know sometimes doctors need to find a physical cause for things, so I hope I'm not making your job harder by being so healthy! It's just just me being a little too active, I suppose. Is that what you were looking for?

When you have this need to keep moving and puttering, do you feel any inner sense of restlessness or discomfort—like an urge inside that makes you feel you must move—or is it just that your body naturally wants to be active without any uncomfortable feeling driving it?

Well, it's... it's certainly not an uncomfortable feeling, not like a pain or anything dreadful. I wouldn't call it discomfort. It's more just... a little wiggle, I suppose? 

Like, when I'm at the senior center meetings, or sitting through the long announcements at church, I just get this... this sort of ants-in-my-chair feeling. It's nothing serious, really! I just find myself needing to shift around a bit, or maybe I'll stand up to get a cup of coffee, or just straighten up the papers on the table in front of me... just little things to help me get through the sitting part. 

It's just a natural urge to be a bit useful and active, not a bad feeling at all. I hope that doesn't make me sound like a disruption to the others? I try to be very quiet about it. Does that sound like a normal way to feel at my age?

When you get that 'ants-in-my-chair' feeling you mentioned, does moving around or changing position actually make that feeling go away, or does it stay pretty much the same whether you're moving or sitting still?

Oh, well, yes, moving certainly helps! It's not that I'm uncomfortable, you understand, but when I just... get up and do something, like fetching that coffee or straightening a cushion, the little wiggly feeling just goes right away. 

It's really quite helpful, honestly. Once I've moved about a bit, I can sit back down and be perfectly attentive again. It just sort of... refreshes me, I suppose. So it definitely doesn't stay the same, no. Getting up fixes it right up. 

I hope that's the right sort of answer? I wouldn't want you to think I'm just wandering around for no good reason! It really does help me settle back down. Is that what usually happens for people?
